Phases of subtle weak phases in $B^0_s\to K^+K^-$ decays depend on the duration of the $B^0_s$ state, which we quantify as $\delta$, ranging from $0$ (coherent) to $\pi/2$ (incoherent). Calculations based on quark-level assumptions provide the potential sources of $\delta$, including the influence of $K^+K^-$ initial and final state interactions, as well as $C\bot S$ terms. Estimates suggest that the average $\delta$ could be around $0.15\pi$ due to $C\bot S$ effects. Moreover, we propose two methods to determine $\delta$ by analyzing (i) $B^0_s\to K^+K^-$ decay time distributions or (ii) $C\perp S$ asymmetries in $B^0_s\to \phi\phi$ decays, both of which are feasible in the LHCb experiment with its existing data.

This research paper examines the approximate solution to a distributed regulation issue governed by a parabolic equation with noise, focusing on the optimal control of a second-generation transport equation with a random initial data. Unlike previous studies, we do not assume the initial data has a high level of regularity. Instead, we use a random field approach to model the initial condition, which allows us to demonstrate the uniqueness of the solution to the transport equation and its corresponding control equation. Furthermore, we show that the approximate solution to the regulation issue converges to the actual solution when the discretization error tends to zero.

Our research examined the size of cosmic-ray fluctuations detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory above 4 EeV through the study of extensive air showers initiated by high-energy particles interacting with the atmosphere. Due to the Earth blocking the direct observation of these particles, scientists use extensive air showers to study their properties. The observed fluctuations in cosmic particles can be reflected in the characteristics of extensive air showers, particularly in the signal recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory's Toya Array, specifically the fluctuations in the electric potential of the Toya Array's antennas. Our analysis focused on the inherent fluctuations inherent to the cosmic neutrino component, while controlling for background levels of cosmic rays. We found the average fluctuation in the total signal amplitude to be 1.63 (plus/minus 0.03) times the average signal caused by cosmic rays, with a 6 sigma level of significance. We also extracted the standard deviation of the distribution of fluctuation sizes as 0.53 (plus/minus 0.10). These findings are highly relevant to the design of future, larger Toya Array detectors that will be part of the Pierre Auger Upgrade.
This paper proves that any variation of Zinbiel algebras automatically becomes an abelian algebra when using the definition from [6, 2].

This study provides the first detailed examination of LHC collisions, specifically Pb-Pb ones at 5.02 TeV, regarding the angle-dependent behavior of stream fluctuations. Researchers studied collisions at different detector angles relative to the initial particle velocity direction, using the ALICE detector at the LHC. They found that the angle of the stream fluctuations varies depending on the collision angle, and this variation correlates with the initial velocity angle. This correlation was confirmed using two different methods. Furthermore, the magnitude of the stream fluctuations was found to be in line with model predictions, specifically the four-flow hypothesis and the hadro-chemical transport model, MUSIC, assuming an isotropic initial condition.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore suitable methods for managing inconsistent data meeting basic consistency criteria. We examine the possibility of maintaining data quality through the application of fix functions, which convert inconsistent data to consistent information according to defined norms. In addition, we investigate the potential benefits of using key attributes to reduce the range of acceptable data configurations. Our main contribution is a systematic analysis of data correction strategies that incorporate fix functions and key attributes to minimize deviations from desired data standards. This analysis reveals the impact of these methods on data consistency, completeness, and accuracy. We also consider the effects of incorporating fix functions and key attributes on data quality by examining various discrepancy management scenarios. These scenarios include scenarios with nominal, ordinal, and interval relationships, as well as those that take into account the likelihood of data entries being true or false. Our research demonstrates the importance of selecting appropriate fix functions and key attributes to achieve optimal results, in accordance with defined performance metrics. Furthermore, we provide a detailed examination of a real-world application involving the analysis of customer reviews, as well as a theoretical solution for extending our approach to handle more complex scenarios with multiple layers of relationships.

This study presents a novel dynamic modeling approach for count-based time series,
building on the foundations of autoregressive models. Our new model, TVPAR, addresses
limitations in current models by allowing parameters to change over time, enabling
further analysis of the statistical properties of the process. We establish conditions
for stationarity, establish the consistency of maximum likelihood estimation, and prove
the consistency of the parameter estimation under a misspecification scenario. TVPAR
can be estimated via a Newton-Raphson method, and the theoretical convergence rate
of this estimator has been established. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical
feasibility of our model through applications to real-world data.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
integrates both category-level and instance-specific representations to facilitate
manipulation tasks across different object categories. This representation, which
is inherently invariant to SE(3), is obtained using a 6D dense point cloud network,
and we demonstrate its effectiveness for tasks like grasping and placing, without
requiring explicit object categories in its training. NDFs comprise two components:
a category-level representation (descriptors) and an instance-specific component (
fields). We train both components together, leveraging a novel loss function that
integrates both a descriptor-based category-level loss and an instance segmentation
loss. Through extensive experiments on the B-Manipulation Dataset, our method
demonstrates superior performance for object recognition, and high success rates for
grasping and placing tasks. In addition, we found it to be highly successful for
recognizing individual objects within a category, even when trained solely on
category-level data. All code and models are available at: https://github.com/google/ndf.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classical statistics. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to compare the performance of different optimization methods for minimizing a given function. This comparison often leverages the concavity of the function in question, whose second-order derivatives indicate the rate at which the optimal solution changes in response to fluctuations. For a specific class of functions known as symmetric and submodular matrices, the concavity of these functions can be ensured by comparing the smallest and largest eigenvalue of matrix embeddings, specifically in a high-dimensional setting where the eigenvalues are continuously distributed. To compare optimization methods for solving linear programming, an alternative comparison involves the concavity of the objective function after transforming the variables through a monotic mapping, whose properties rely on the angle between the original and transformed variable directions. This work investigates the concavity of the Bethe free energy in the context of satisfiability problems, a well-studied benchmark problem in machine learning, and validates the results of previous studies based on detailed perturbation analyses of the TAP equations. Additionally, this work develops a novel proof of the concavity of the Bethe free energy, demonstrating the concavity of the TAP free energy near the phase transition threshold for a specific model, including random K-satisfiability (RK-SAT) and random 3-satisfiability (R3-SAT). The detection of extra-galactic planets and aerosol gratings from UV stellar spectra holds significant promise in sourcing data for planetary science and stellar physics. However, considering the complexities involved in analyzing these spectra, the number of solid detections remains limited. Notwithstanding this challenge, the assumption that aerosol assessments are inherently difficult has been disproven, as the fundamental physics governing planetary systems and stellar physics can be accurately represented through a small number of parameters, thereby facilitating analysis. Meanwhile, the amount of relevant stellar spectral data continues to grow, thanks to mission extensions and improved sensing technologies. Consequently, the number of detected planets and the level of dust particle characterization are likely to increase significantly. For example, future observations from the James Webb Space Telescope will produce an abundance of high-resolution spectra, requiring precise assessment of aerosols to minimize the loss of valuable astronomical data.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based software for Generalized Graphical Lasso
computation. Generalized Graphical Lasso extends the well-known Lasso regression
and Graphical Lasso estimation beyond continuous outcomes to account for outcomes
that may follow Generalized Linear Models, including logistic, Poisson, and
inverse linear models. We offer a command for estimating the corresponding inverse
weight matrix under the assumption of no dependence among the outcomes. In addition
to default settings, users can tailor the estimation process to their data by
specifying variables, models, penalty values, convergence criteria, and more. We
also include a selection of algorithms users may utilize or combine, including
BPDGLasso, BCGD, BCGD+, IterShrinkage, fixed point, and Newton's method, as well
as multi-core processing and sparse inverse matrices as output. We provide an
associated test suite to guarantee correctness and benchmark the library using a
variety of datasets.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving configurational stability in molecular systems are considered, and a comparative assessment of their effectiveness and necessary computational expense is performed, leading to the development of advanced Metropolis sampling techniques. By utilizing Langevin dynamics, a suite of advanced configurational sampling methods that combine deterministic steps with probability-weighted choices is introduced, resulting in optimized strategies for addressing complex scenarios with multiple interconnected minima and chemically relevant timescales. The new methods, including an optimized version of the "thin" Metropolis algorithm, significantly boost the efficiency of configurational sampling by multiple orders of magnitude, and the developed frameworks are suitable for integration with existing numerical methods, enabling the application of configurational sampling to a broad range of problems, including the optimization of potential energy surfaces, stochastic thermalization, and biased sampling techniques.

Understanding the dynamics of complex networks relies heavily on analyzing significant nodes, especially in scenarios where critical information spreads quickly. Research has focused on identifying pivotal nodes in single-layer networks, yet real-world situations are often better represented by multilayer models, accounting for information across multiple platforms. Here, we develop a method to determine the significance of nodes in multilayer networks by combining the method of current topics in bilingual corpora, essentially treating each layer as a separate linguistic context. This approach enables the identification of prominent nodes and their associated meanings across each layer. Notably, our approach can be adapted for an adaptive version that accounts for changes in node significance over time, captured by an operator that reflects reliance between layers. This adaptive version, in turn, is valuable for analyzing the impact of individual layers on the significance of nodes in other layers. We apply this method to an empirical analysis of a collaborative network throughout the course of a year, thereby demonstrating its utility in network evolution studies.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study utilizes high-speed imaging to examine spheres interacting with a fluid surface in a confined setting, with results shown for spheres moving through the surface from both below and above, as well as for partially immersed spheres subjected to various flow velocities. A critical category of water entry known as the "liquid seal" phase, characterized by the formation of a tight ring around the sphere's equator, has been identified. The period of seal duration varies greatly, extending from less than 0.1ms in high-speed impacts to hundreds of ms in slower encounters. A distinctive pattern of ring break occurred in the seal phase, with spheres moving faster than 10m/s often experiencing ring break outside of the equatorial region. The duration of seal is influenced by the velocity at which the sphere enters the surface, as well as its initial distance from the surface, with deeper starting points resulting in shorter seal durations. Furthermore, relationships have been established to describe the distance the sphere travels during seal, as well as its final distance from the surface following water entry.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an extensive range of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. The range of these theories can be broadly classified based on the entropy of extremal black holes, ranging from low entropy hues of the $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity core, through to higher entropy configurations characterized by both scalar fields and extensive Calabi-Yau geometry, to high entropy configurations akin to $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity. The role of theta-terms, which introduce holomorphic operators into the effective action, was examined, with our results indicating that they are necessary for validating the consistency of the effective theories at a quantum level. Our calculations using first-principles methods have investigated the properties of cupricite CuFe2S3.  This material is notable for consisting of close-packed sulfur layers surrounded by copper and iron, and we found that its electronic structure can be understood by focusing on a small supercell.  Through further analysis of a larger unit cell, we identified localized electrons associated with iron and decoupled spin moments, confirming experimental findings.  However, in smaller unit cells, decoupling is absent due to electron interaction, and we attribute this lack of decoupling to iron within gamma-site rather than delta-site.  Our results also reveal that decoupling is possible at high temperatures due to weakened electron interaction.

Weak coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations in solids generally prevents the formation of excitons with opposite spins from combining with phonons, which limits the availability of phonon-driven periodic transformations. However, there is a specific scenario where intense light forces spin-symmetric excitons and a specific phonon mode to shift their relative phase, leading to huge Rabi oscillations even at low intensities. This phenomenon is particularly uncommon and we demonstrate its occurrence in particular systems characterized by strong coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations. This result opens the door for extremely intense, light-driven periodic transformations in materials with strong electron-phonon interactions.

Our investigation focuses on the adjustable Dirac points in a two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper structure lattice. By adjusting the magnitude of the next-nearest neighbor hoppings from 10% to 90% of the nearest neighbor hoppings, significant topological changes occur. Initially, the lattice exhibits a topological insulator behavior, characterized by an adjustment of the Berry curvature distribution around the two adjustable Dirac points. As the ratio of the next-nearest to nearest neighbor hoppings increases beyond 1, the lattice transitions into a topological metal state, displaying an intriguing redistribution of the Berry curvature and consequent merging of the two adjustable Dirac points. Our proposed design involves a rectangular array of Mn atoms, situated above a pentaagonal lattice of phosphorus, where the magnitude of the hoppings can be accurately controlled through application of strain, voltage, or magnetism, thereby allowing for practical manipulation of the Dirac points.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states can be generated through quantum-optical catalysis using a beam splitter, a phase mask, and a container holding photon-number-state "keys." These states are characterized by controlled photon populations and coherent wave functions, making them suitable for demonstrating quantum supremacy in optomechanical systems. A proposed experimental setup, verified through numerical simulations, utilizes laser light and employs quantum catalysis to create these states, which could serve as benchmarks for evaluating the quantum performance of optomechanical systems.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Weyl's curvature tensor equation. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of how the Weyl curvature tensor's bivector components help determine the solution to the Einstein field equations, especially in the presence of an electromagnetic field. A comprehensive examination is given of how the Newman-Penrose formalism works, with particular attention paid to the role of bivectors within this framework. A concise overview is also provided of the underlying mathematical framework, including the complex differential equation component.

A significant hurdle in developing effective linear learning models for chemical compounds arises from the constraint that atomic proportions must add up to unity. This challenge is particularly pronounced in modeling polymers, as their definitions inherently require integer multiples of repeating units. To overcome this issue, a new method has been developed which employs a two-step approach: first, a linear regression model is used to predict approximate atomic proportions, and then these estimates are refined through an integer optimization algorithm that incorporates the definition of the polymer in question. The proposed technique has been effectively demonstrated in predicting the structures of nanotubes and graphites, and also extends the applicability of machine learning models to all chemical polymers.

We introduce a novel medical image segmentation technique, known as Dense Attention Unet, which incorporates both channel and spatial attention mechanisms to enhance performance. This method leverages dense attention to further enhance the framework, achieving superior results in esophageal tumor segmentation from CT images. Esophageal tumor segmentation is a complex task that involves distinguishing healthy esophageal tissue from abnormal regions, making it crucial for accurate surgical planning, neoplasm size calculations, and positioning of radiotherapy equipment. Despite its importance, automated segmentation of esophageal tumors remains challenging due to varying neoplasm shapes, close proximity to surrounding blood vessels, and limited contrast in CT images. To address this, we propose a multi-resolution DDAUnet approach, utilizing large convolutional filters to capture distant features and small filters to detect border neoplasm regions. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of experiments on a publicly available dataset, showing its superiority over existing techniques.

Multilingual communities, being proficient in two or more languages, pose significant challenges in categorizing their preferred writing systems. Some may use code-switching, blending two languages together, while others prefer code-mixed approaches, blending two different writing systems, such as switching between Latin and Devanagari scripts. Although significant progress has been made in both multilingual speech and writing tasks, significant obstacles remain. For instance, there is a lack of standardized notation systems to represent multilingual writing, making it difficult to develop effective neural networks. Furthermore, multilingual data sets are often disparate, complicating attempts to combine them. Additionally, there are issues with linguistic analysis, such as the difficulty of modeling code-mixed syntax and semantics, not to mention the problem of evaluating systems against unclear evaluation metrics. This paper delves into the complexities of multilingual NLP, outlining potential solutions, such as using universal character sets, integrating disparate data sets, and developing code-mixed syntax and semantics, as well as highlighting ongoing research efforts and promising areas for future investigation.

Describing images automatically has become a sophisticated task for computers, with several techniques proposed to achieve this goal. Evaluating the effectiveness of these methods is crucial, and a widely accepted metric for this purpose is the similarity between an automatic image description and a set of reference descriptions provided by humans. Nevertheless, using human references in this context presents a few challenges, such as the risk of overfitting to individual descriptions rather than the underlying picture representation, and the difficulty of accumulating a representative and compact set of references. In an attempt to address these issues, this study introduces two novel approaches, one utilizing a single human reference description to evaluate descriptions automatically, and another incorporating a batch of references through a selective attention mechanism, both demonstrated through experiments involving existing automatic image description generation models, with notable improvements in their performance.

Tantalum oxide in its form of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is an intriguing material with multiple crystal structures resulting from different preparation methods. We found that by subjecting Ta$_2$O$_5$ to varying levels of oxygen content and applying pressure, we could replicate existing data and predict the natural state of the material. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we were able to compare theoretical results with experimental data, including the location of foreign atoms and defects. However, the actual Ta$_2$O$_5$ bulk state proves elusive, and we are left with multiple possible structures, not counting the polymorphic types mentioned in the study.

User profiles on social media platforms can be influenced by geographic factors, such as the location where they received their education, which reflect underlying cultural characteristics. These aspects shape users' perceptions, including their susceptibility to believing misinformation. Investigating a subset of Reddit users from the United States, we found that users from different educational backgrounds based on ZIP codes exhibit distinct information-sharing behaviors. Notably, users with higher education degrees tend to disseminate more misinformation than those with lower education levels. This pattern holds true even after accounting for variables such as income, political affiliation, and online engagement. Furthermore, users from educational 'deserts' are more likely to share misinformation, suggesting that cultural factors play a significant role in this phenomenon. Our study highlights the significance of considering the complex interplay between geographic, cultural, and online variables that influence the spread of misinformation on a large scale.

Humans use a variety of sounds to communicate efficiently, beyond language, which is evident from the vast array of sounds produced during cooking, sports, or other activities. Despite this complexity, research on sound patterns has been largely focused on simple tones and music. This study undertakes a more nuanced investigation of sound patterns made by humans instructing each other in a robotic setup. Using Fourier analysis and metrics from machine learning, we demonstrated the sounds produced for different tasks and within the same task contain distinct features. By applying multiclass support vector machines and random forests, we found that sounds generated for different tasks and similar sounds from the same task can be accurately classified (above 80% and 90% accuracy respectively). This study reveals the high capacity for sounds to express information and a potential limitation in the range of sounds that can be represented. This research was part of a broader effort to develop a learning model for following manipulation instructions given in a natural, spoken language.

A set of sophisticated fluid dynamics equations, specifically Euler-Arnold equations, has been uncovered that underlie the complex dynamics of conformal field theory at its critical point. These equations, characterized by a non-abelian Lie group G, capture the intricate motions of local operators within the QFT framework and reveal their intricate interactions through exchange of particles, a phenomenon that underlies conformal field theory's fundamental structure. By employing a new, advanced fluid dynamics approach, the intricate movements of operator algebras are represented as complex, high-dimensional fluid motions that give rise to intricate movements of particles. This novel representation exposes the internal workings of conformal field theory's complex dynamics and uncovers the intricate movements of particles that underlie the non-abelian operator algebra of a d=2 CFT through a higher-dimensional fluid dynamics model. This model has been tested against the results of three precise CFT tests, namely the Ising, SOS, and ASP models.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with their own language abilities are now commonplace, incorporating features like natural text input, dialog systems, and automated operation. Due to the complex nature of these systems, manual testing is no longer sufficient, and a automated testing method is crucial for ensuring the proper functioning of these systems. A novel approach to testing conversational systems has been presented in this paper, incorporating a range of techniques including formal methods, dynamic analysis, and machine learning. This approach has been applied to a real-world scenario, specifically the testing of a Amazon Mechanical Turk-based bot, and the results obtained have been discussed. The proposed approach has been found to be an cost-effective and efficient solution for testing conversational systems and can be further improved by integrating additional techniques.

Cross-domain recommendation has seen significant progress in recent years, but it still faces a major challenge: most current methods rely heavily on data from multiple domains, which can lead to scalability issues when domains are numerous. Additionally, many existing techniques fail to utilize user feedback effectively, particularly in multi-sparsity domains, where both items and users can be sparse. In such environments, recommendations often prioritize users with more feedback over those with less, undermining fairness. This study introduces a novel FairMultiSDCR framework that addresses these problems by leveraging user feedback more efficiently and achieving a balance between item selection and user fairness. Specifically, FairMultiSDCR enhances user representations by incorporating attribute preferences and reducing bias caused by sparsity. When compared to state-of-the-art methods, FairMultiSDCR significantly enhances the fairness and efficiency of recommendations in multi-sparsity domains, as demonstrated by the experimental results.

Conic optimization is a highly effective tool for resolving complex issues involving polynomial inequalities when used in conjunction with nonlinear programming. Conic formulations can sometimes overcome inefficiencies in traditional nonlinear programming methods due to their ability to handle inequalities through geometric transformations, thereby overcoming limitations associated with nonconvex nonlinear programming. Despite the benefits, there are obstacles to employing this strategy on a large scale, primarily due to the difficulty of creating conic formulations and solving large-scale models. This paper presents Hypatia - a new Julia-based package for creating conic formulations - that enables users to easily formulate problems involving multivariate polynomial inequalities and share them on a large scale, as well as extract efficient solver options, without requiring extensive computational expertise.

The escalating use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in neuroscience research and clinical applications has generated a significant amount of data, making it crucial to develop efficient and automated image analysis techniques. However, MRI acquisitions are often affected by quality control issues, leading to poor image data that researchers and medical professionals must identify and exclude from analyses. Although various deep learning-based techniques are now applied to MRI post-processing, there's limited research on developing models that can automatically detect substandard MRI images across different sites and scanners. This paper proposes a novel strategy for training MRI image quality assessment models, drawing on theories from multi-task learning and group selection algebra, in order to achieve robust models that can effectively evaluate the quality of new, unseen MRI images acquired with different sequences and scanners. The proposed method is demonstrated through a practical application using publicly available MRI data sets from various sources, including the Neuro Imaging Informatics Commons. The results show that the proposed model achieves superior performance in predicting the ratings of MRI image quality when compared to existing techniques. Moreover, the model exhibits excellent generalization performance in distinguishing high-quality and low-quality MRI images based on reader-specific knowledge, without requiring explicit supervision. The code for this study is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghafoorimr/MRI-QA.

To assess the impact of private electric vehicles on a distribution network's stability and to identify optimal charging management strategies, this paper develops a mathematical framework that takes into account various factors such as network resilience, vehicle charging costs, and charging limitations. Utilizing multi-agent optimization theory, the study transforms complex individual objectives into decentralized, agent-based decisions that can be made through simple local calculations. This leads to a decentralized, efficient charging management plan that balances individual and collective interests. Numerical analyses of real-world scenarios with different network conditions, electric vehicle specifications, and charging policies demonstrate the effects of private electric vehicles on distribution network stability and provide actionable insights for policymakers and operators looking to promote resilient and environmentally friendly transportation solutions.

An intriguing model has been presented, consisting of multiple agents meeting within an infinite-timeframe setting, where they work towards a common goal together.
The model features agents that move independently, with no restrictions other than maintaining physical contact.
To encourage collaborative behavior, a reward system was designed, awarding agents for working together and penalizing them for independent action-taking.
Through rewarding schemes were found to exhibit complex, varied patterns of behavior.
A learning approach was developed, utilizing policy optimization in a way that maximizes future rewards, resulting in cooperative agents.
The model and learning approach were put to the test in simulation environments, demonstrating successful implementation of cooperative policies.
The approach was also applied to a complex meeting problem, where agents had distinct roles and objectives, yielding a notable improvement in performance.
The developed approach was compared to alternative learning methods, revealing its superior performance.
The model and learning approach were further expanded to handle real-world problems, such as traffic congestion and the meeting game with deception.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The study predicts the masses of diverse extra baryons and mesons resulting from a specific theoretical framework, which incorporates a quartic symmetry in the fundamental and adjoint representations of the $SU(3)$ color gauge group. This prediction is based on the analysis of multiple quadratic and linear operators that yield extra mass terms when calculated within the framework. The study focuses on the prediction of extra baryons and mesons, and it is essential to note that for mesons, both bosonic and fermionic results are given, whereas for baryons, only fermionic results are provided. The theoretical framework underlying this prediction is based on the assumption that the fundamental representation of the $SU(3)$ color gauge group is filled to capacity, and the study uses the available data to estimate the scale parameter "$\Lambda$" which determines mass levels. The results reveal that the masses of extra baryons and mesons can range from a few hundred GeV to above 10 TeV, and the study recommends the use of more advanced methods for calculating the mass levels in the future.

The Coxeter groups, which extend the Thompson groups, include three main classes: the I, II, and III types. Recently, it has been proven that the II$_2$ and II$_3$ groups contain numerous invariant subgroups, potentially leading to an abundance of invariant functions under these groups. In a significant advancement, we demonstrate the existence of non-trivial invariant functions within the B$_2$ and B$_3$ Coxeter groups, thereby expanding upon the foundational theorem for these groups.

Utilizing a new method that combines SN Ia photometry and astrophysical lensing theory, we've re-analyzed the Pantheon SN Ia dataset to determine the average amplification caused by weak lensing. With a assumed Gaussian distribution of convergent masses, the resulting average amplification is only slightly higher than expected, around 2%. However, when we assume a lognormal distribution of convergent masses, the average amplification increases significantly, ranging from approximately 10% to nearly 100%. This variation in average amplification affects the cosmological parameters derived from the Pantheon SN Ia dataset, with the assumed distribution of convergent masses leading to different Hubble constant estimates and sometimes even different category assignments based on goodness of fit. Consequently, this study highlights the importance of considering lensing effects in future SN Ia datasets and the need to incorporate a range of possible distributions when analyzing them.

We introduce a novel type of T-shaped junction called a T hub, which is composed of two T-shaped intersections in a 2D silicon-on-insulator material. We investigate the unique propagation of electromagnetic waves within this T hub structure and identify both high-refractive-index regions and low-refractive-index regions where light waves behave differently. Specifically, we find that the behavior of electromagnetic waves in the high-refractive-index regions at the center of the T hub is similar to that in T-shaped intersections, whereas the behavior in the low-refractive-index regions varies based on the phase difference between the input waves and takes on different forms such as light waves interfering with each other, canceling out completely, or forming closed patterns. We also analyze various T hub configurations and suggest a method for creating these structures using stackable photonic chips. Notably, our proposed T hub structure can automatically align the phase of input light waves to a specific state just by adjusting the phase difference between the inputs, which could be useful for phase-based applications.

Context-aware object recognition models can better understand the context of objects within an image, thanks to the advancement of large-scale pre-trained object recognizers using context-free labels. Since many existing datasets for object recognition are based on text descriptions that don't account for context, new resources are necessary to evaluate a model's ability to understand context. We propose a novel assessment of the context-aware ability of these pre-trained recognizers by utilizing existing datasets, incorporating a scoring system to value the context based on surrounding objects, including both positive and negative instances. The proposed assessment technique is applicable to widely used datasets like COCO and VGG2, leading to an observable improvement in context-aware object recognition performance when trained on these datasets.

The main focus of this paper is to examine multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations given by (1.1), particularly in establishing the existence, number, and characteristics of multiplicity of solutions for this system of equations. It is essential to note that this system involves equations with nonlinearity that is capable of incorporating singularities, which such problems typically deal with. Some key results achieved in this study include proof of the existence of multiple solutions for the system of equations, as well as a two-solution theorem. Moreover, this paper simplifies and extends previous work on the singular Trudinger-Moser problem by introducing a new approach that leverages a Kirchhoff type system of equations. The main results of this study are applied to a range of related problems, including a Kirchhoff type equation, a p-Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations, the singular Trudinger-Moser problem, and others.

In the context of negatively correlated binary random variables, we establish a converse to Bernoulli's inequality, which has far-reaching implications. By treating each binary random variable as an independent copy, we gain strong concentration results for their average value. Specifically, for a sequence of independent binary random variables with mean values $\frac{1}{2}$ and a measure of negative correlation captured by the Deviation of Disparity, we obtain concentration bounds in terms of the square of the standard deviation. For a single binary random variable, this yields a strengthened version of Talagrand's concentration inequality. Additionally, we obtain improved concentration bounds for the sum of independent binary random variables with means $\frac{1}{2}$, which can be viewed as a binary version of the Hypercontractivity inequality.

We define symplectic transformations that preserve the boundary and distinguish complex coordinates from their conjugates. These include the rotation of sections in contact manifolds and certain embedding methods. It is proven that any closed, oriented manifold with complex structure can be paired with a specific type of symplectic transformation, resulting in a new closed, oriented manifold with an established metric. This shows that all closed, oriented manifolds with complex structure are pairwise non-distinguishable under symplectic transformations, except for a singular exception - the KP sphere of dimension three.

A newly developed theory called 'ideal acceptance theory' aims to address the underlying mechanisms behind the acceptance of incompatible kidney transplants by the recipient's immune system. This theory emphasizes the importance of a donor-recipient compatibility match, yet also suggests that the immune system can sometimes tolerate certain discrepancies. To better comprehend this interplay, a mathematical model has been created which illustrates how the immune system's tolerance relates to compatibility. This model extends previous ideal acceptance models by incorporating multiple transplantation criteria. A numerical example demonstrates the application of this model in a complex transplantation scenario.

Recent studies using word2vec on financial news have shown representations learned from polarized language learn distinct meanings, supported by analytical techniques revealing two components corresponding to formal and informal language. In contrast, many researchers who use word2vec in financial contexts rely on intuitive arguments, ignoring the potential influence of language variability on learned representations. We contend this practice is flawed as it is based on an untested assumption about word2vec's behavior in response to changing linguistic contexts. Furthermore, we find low-frequency words often ignore the challenge of context variability, mapping words to unique entities without distinguishing between similar words. In the specific case of Loughran-McDonald's word lists, we find the proposed explanation for them is also unfounded, suggesting they are actually a result of word2vec's response to the presence of polarized language rather than company name polarities.

This article presents the basic SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM versions of a previously proposed Waveforming scheme for integrated data and power transfer, also known as WDPT. The original WDPT concept incorporates multiple antennas and OFDM carriers to enable simultaneous data transmission and wireless energy replenishment, with optimizations aimed at maximizing energy transfer and meeting data transfer requirements. The SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM versions of this scheme share similar performance characteristics with the original WDPT, in terms of data transfer rate, energy transfer efficiency, and their respective normalized values. These equivalences hold under various conditions, including those where the base station is powered by the same energy harvesting technology. The corresponding performance benchmarks for all four versions of the WDPT scheme are determined through numerical calculations.

This research introduces a hybrid level-set/embedded boundary method to model boundary dynamics occurring during phase changes, while bypassing issues related to point sources and the level-set grid interference. Since no explicit representation of boundaries is necessary, overhangs resulting from numerical errors are permitted, despite requiring additional treatment to prevent them from settling into crevices. A numerical scheme is developed to solve the Navier--Stokes equations in a variable domain, and a bond line model is introduced to eliminate overhangs. Computational examples demonstrate the technique's effectiveness in modeling both linear and nonlinear solid--liquid interactions.

In multiagent learning settings beyond Nash equilibria, rationalizable behavior is desired, meaning agents make decisions based on correct incentives and without false offers. For general games, learning Nash equilibria via reinforcement learning can result in unnecessary exploration due to the false moves made in response to irrelevant actions, whereas learning rationalizable equilibria avoids this issue. In the case of user equilibrium (UE) games, which are a special class of games where agents make decisions under constraints and have complete private information, we can learn rationalizable equilibria using reinforcement learning without an explicit knowledge of the system dynamics. This is achieved by utilizing neural networks to predict the rationalizable equilibrium actions directly from the observation, without the need for exploration-exploitation tradeoffs. We prove that the proposed method learns a rationalizable equilibrium action in the limit as the learning period approaches infinity, under certain conditions. We also conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for learning UE equilibria in various large-scale traffic networks.

This study examines how preventive network damage, in the form of reducing connections between individuals, affects the spread of an epidemic in a variable network. We developed an epidemic model that takes into account the removal of connections and the progression of the epidemic, which is applied to a random network that changes based on the epidemic's impact. We found that preventing network fragmentation is key to controlling the spread of an epidemic, but this strategy can backfire in some cases, accelerating the epidemic's pace instead. The probability of an epidemic breaking out, as well as its duration, were both found to be influenced by the condition under which new connections are formed. We developed a rough guide to managing epidemics through network manipulation, which includes maintaining multiple connections that can be easily added or removed, as well adapting the formation of new connections to change in accordance with the epidemic's progression.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately determining physical parameters in theoretical frameworks. While incorporating inconsistent units and systemic differences is a common challenge, a well-structured framework can streamline this process by providing a unified framework for data and a coherent scheme for parameter fitting. In the context of identifying fundamental properties in a certain theoretical framework, an example dataset has been created that includes experimental outcomes converted to consistent units. This dataset serves as the input for a conventional PDF fitting method. By dividing constraints into physical and mathematical categories, a customized solver can effectively handle the fitting process. A notable aspect of this approach is that it maintains the integrity of the theoretical variables during the fitting process, ensuring that the final solutions remain within the valid range of the variables.

To improve policy performance in challenging real-world applications, reinforcement learning agents can pair experience replay with off-policy learning methods. However, retrieving meaningful information from diverse and potentially noisy memories poses a significant difficulty. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new variance decrease based experience replay framework that prioritizes memories according to the uncertainty surrounding their utility. Specifically, the agency is trained to minimize the entropy of future experiences expected to be derived from the memory, allowing it to selectively focus on the most informative data. By adjusting the exploration-exploitation tradeoff, the agent can switch between the following strategies: selecting memories with a high probability of leading to beneficial outcomes (useful memories), choosing memories that provide specific knowledge (target memories), or selecting memories that offer generalization capabilities (general memories). The proposed approach is validated through experiments conducted on various reinforcement learning tasks.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of responses generated, we introduce 
a new metric called Branch Accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a simple continuation 
branching mechanism to simulate real-world conversations. Our proposed method, 
known as MultiTalk, incorporates a mix of sequence-level and instance-level 
decoding objectives to produce more natural responses while managing branching 
expenditure. Throughout our research, we utilized short segments of the MultiTalk 
Dataset. Our results on the full dataset demonstrate significant gains in both 
Diversity and Branching Expense when compared to standard generation methods.

We present a series of fast N-body simulations spanning various altered gravity scenarios, specifically those where the gravitational force is modified in relation to mass and density, while keeping the speed of gravity constant. This allows for convenient scaling of simulations across different systems by maintaining conformity with Einstein's theory of gravity. Although these simulations were initially conducted to examine altered gravity models, they now provide a useful tool for exploring the consequences of modified gravity through the equivalent mass-shelf parameter, even though this parameter varies throughout our simulations. A direct comparison with existing altered gravity simulations, which were created using more detailed numerical simulations but have a less extensive range of mass variations, is also possible. Given the speed of our N-body method, we are able to perform an extensive examination of how dark matter behaves under various altered gravity scenarios, including models that exhibit oscillations and those with significant growth rates of density perturbations. A simple analytical approach is also developed to quickly determine the properties of these scenarios through the equivalent mass-shelf parameter, allowing for the exploration of altered gravity scenarios through the behavior of density perturbations.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Toda lattice on the positive reals, respectively. These interpretations extend the relationship between SLE and Gaussian free fields initially discovered by Miller and Sheffield.

MediaWiki's robust functionality extends beyond its underlying architecture, resulting from its adaptation for high-traffic sites like Wikipedia. Originally developed to meet the needs of a centralized project like Wikipedia, MediaWiki's features may appear opposite to what is desired for collaborative research, where transparency and process disclosure are crucial. Nevertheless, MediaWiki's versatility offers several benefits, including the visibility of calculation methods, study design, and raw data, which can be particularly valuable in collective research. By simplifying the integration of external tools and applications, MediaWiki can be an attractive base for developing customized collaborative research platforms. Following an analysis of the existing open source code, the WorkingWiki project was established to ease the transition from Wikipedia to independent research projects by providing a customizable platform based on MediaWiki.

A linearized model is developed to study the dynamics of turbulent jet fires under acoustic disturbances. In this model, which relies on active flame dynamics, a specific approach is taken to analyze flame response based on hydrodynamics and chemistry interactions. To apply this method, a detailed examination of active flame models and the sources of acoustics in jet fires are reviewed, considering combustion instability and flame response to vibration. A linearized conservation equation is formulated, and the acoustic source term is derived using an active flame method. To validate the model, comparisons with previous studies on jet fires are conducted, and an analysis of its stability is performed. Furthermore, the model's behavior under both open and closed systems is investigated. A numerical example demonstrates the model's effectiveness by examining the response of a jet fire to acoustic forcing within a closed system.

We investigate the neutrino-induced processes that arise from the ultralight dark matter field interacting with neutrinos within the context of a non-ULDM Poisson-type equation. By assuming that a small amount of dark matter participates in a $\theta$-$\phi$ oscillation, we determine the ultralight dark matter mass range that could contribute to $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay and test it against existing and future experiments. Furthermore, we examine the validity of the hypothesis within the parameters of cosmological stability and determine the ultralight dark matter mass range that could influence the matter power spectrum.

We introduce a novel nonlocal gravity theory where mass and energy are related to specific nonlocal Tetrads, which are composed of the metric and electromagnetic field. By utilizing the metric structure, we derive the nonlocal Einstein field equations in a compact, closed form. These equations are equivalent to a set of nonlinear differential equations that the nonlocal Tetrads must satisfy. Our approach provides a nonlocal generalization of Einstein's gravity theory and offers a consistent framework for understanding the behavior of gravitational fields at all scales.

Understanding how the human genome influences specific traits or developments is a complex task involving numerous factors, including the two mentioned above. On one hand, we have the detailed, element-level analysis of 2.7 million genomic segments across the human genome, which provides a rich source of information on how the genome functions and its impact on traits or developments. On the other hand, we have large-scale association studies that have been conducted on a vast population of 125,000 individuals and cover the majority of the human genome. By integrating and comparing these two sources of information, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of 18 human characteristics or developments, including obesity, metabolism, blood type, and various diseases. By linking specific genomic elements to characteristics or developments, we have gained valuable insights into their functional impact and the potential risks and benefits of variations in the genome. Furthermore, we have made available a public platform that houses this integrated information for future reference and analysis.

The introduction discusses the significance of investigating subleading theoretical effects in particle collisions, which can lead to precise tests of QCD and its extensions.
The paper focuses on a specific category of subleading phenomena, namely those arising from the collisions of charged and neutral hadrons in the LHC's detector, and discusses potential sources of these events including dark matter, long-lived particles, and leptoquarks.
It is essential to identify and exclude these subleading processes or determine their properties, and for this purpose, new approaches are being developed to analyze minor systems in the context of various experiments and scenarios, such as with the ALICE detector at the CERN LHC and in beyond Standard Model scenarios involving dark matter and leptoquarks.
The paper also explores current limitations and potential workarounds in searching for these subleading processes.
The appendices provide detailed information on long-lived particle signatures and on certain BSM models involving leptoquarks and dark matter.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of activity. To challenge this concept, we calculated the expected interval between which a neutron star binary system would display X-ray activity again and return to a state of inactivity, based on the established parameters of such systems and the theoretical models of their behavior. According to our calculations, even the longest observed period of inactivity would need to repeat within the next hundred thousand years, suggesting that many of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center are actually made up of neutron star binaries rather than black holes.

The exact understanding of electrons interacting with vibrations in solids has been complicated by the influence of inertia. Although Lagrangians describe these interactions effectively, the underlying mechanical aspects, stemming from the Einstein's equivalence principle, can impact electron behavior in solids, particularly at high speeds or in solid-state phenomena with large strain energies. By applying relativistic and classical mechanics principles, the electron-phonon interaction has been re-examined in this study. The results show that inertia influences the interaction, potentially leading to significant effects on spin-vibration coupling, electron orbital motion, and lattice distortion. The role of the Ricci scalar from general relativity also becomes relevant in this context. Consequently, the magnitude of the interaction can vary significantly, potentially leading to novel phenomena induced by solid-state objects or situations that generate gravitational fields, as seen in materials with solid-electrolyte interfaces or nanosecond-pulse laser-induced strain energies.

Humans engage in conversations with diverse aims, which are often driven by the underlying intentions and underlying meaning behind their words. To evaluate the effectiveness of conversational agents, we believe it is crucial to examine their ability to understand the semantic objectives behind statements, rather than just measuring their surface-level accuracy. To support this claim and provide a meaningful assessment of conversational agents, we present a new challenge that incorporates the Natural Language Inference task to gauge the semantic varieties of commands issued by the agents. In this challenge, systems are tasked with generating commands that can be classified under broad categories by natural language processing models, which require an understanding of the underlying semantics. We also introduce a new dataset consisting of 100 instruction sets, each containing 20 related commands, for the Natural Language Inference task. This dataset is an advancement over existing datasets that typically incorporate individual commands rather than instruction sets. Our findings indicate that the performance of conversational agents on this task is significantly lower than their performance on traditional evaluation methods that focus solely on the surface level of commands. According to our analysis, the current limitations of conversational agents are due to their lack of understanding of the semantic objectives behind commands. To validate this hypothesis, we connected a conversational agent to natural language processing models and observed a noticeable improvement in performance. Our challenge and dataset are available online at https://yichun.sh/conv-nli/.

Theoretical models of rotating substellar bodies have been comprehensively calculated using computational code, covering a range of masses and compositions. These models, for objects with surface temperatures below 2500K, incorporate the effects of metallicity, pressure, and surface gravity on density and composition. Based on these calculations, we define the boundaries within which objects of a particular mass and composition can exist and stable for which fluctuations do not cause them to shed mass or experience internal instability. These results provide essential information for interpreting observations of protostellar disks and the properties of extraterrestrial objects with masses similar to those of planets like 51 Eri b.

The analysis of amplitude data from laboratory experiments that simulate gravitational waves is crucial for detecting gravitational waves generated by gravitational waves. However, interpreting such data involves addressing various technical challenges. One significant issue is comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions, especially when the effects of uncertainties in amplitude measurements are considered. The current method uses a minimum detection threshold in the amplitude spectrum above background noise. However, this approach doesn't effectively take into account the uncertainties associated with the amplitude of individual signals. A more sophisticated technique involves using a likelihood function that considers the probability of exceeding a certain signal amplitude, and is therefore a more comprehensive method for comparing data with theoretical predictions. Additionally, this approach facilitates the incorporation of uncertainties in amplitude measurements and noise levels. A numerical strategy has been developed to implement this method by simulating the effects of signal and noise in amplitude measurements. This method has been applied to data from broadband non-coherent searches for binary black hole mergers.

A comprehensive model has been developed to describe the progression of gravitational waves from binary massive objects. The model, which considers a generic model of gravitational waves produced by binary mergers, includes predictions for the power and spectrum of gravitational waves over time. The model comprises seven components with varying dynamics, including an initial phase of intense energy emission, a phase with decreasing energy signals, a phase with decreasing frequency signals, a phase of energetic particle production, a phase of cooling particles, a phase of cooling electrons, and a phase of exhausted energy sources. The model has been applied to describe the progression of energy signals from binary mergers of different masses, including neutron stars and black holes, as observed with gravitational waves. The model has also been used to describe the progression of energy signals from gamma-ray burst afterglows, which involve the interaction of energetic particles with the surrounding environment, such as dust and gas. The model has been tested against a wide range of observational data from gamma-ray burst afterglows, which provide insights into their physical properties, including the characteristics of their sources, the density of the surrounding environment, and the characteristics of the particles involved. The model has significant potential for further development, including the incorporation of additional physical processes and variations in the properties of the sources and the surrounding environment, as well as the prediction of new phenomena that may arise from the interaction of particles with the environment, such as the production of high-energy particles and the modulation of gamma-ray burst pulses.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a two-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across separate lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. This representation helps clarify complex data by minimizing overlap and enhancing readability. However, as the number of connections between pairs of elements grows, the resulting graph may become poorly scaled for visualization, necessitating a reduction in the intensity of these connections. In response, we introduce a new technique called Bipartite Vertex Division (BVD), which strengthens connections between pairs of elements by inserting additional edges between their counterparts, thus providing a alternative representation that can be more compact. In this study, we outline BVD's characteristics, identify instances of bipartite graphs that can be represented using division, and determine a key parameter indicating the level of connection strength. Additionally, we address the challenge of determining BVD's parameter for a given bipartite graph, discovering that this task is feasible in a time that grows in proportion to the square of the number of edges, and demonstrating the applicability of BVD to problems involving the visualization of bipartite graphs.

This research focuses on analyzing biologically-inspired bipedal gait dynamics to optimize a robotic leg design for a specific mission, where a robot experiences low gravity and needs to maintain stability and conserve propellant by taking large steps. To achieve this, we developed a simplified model of a robotic leg with a propellant storage and release mechanism, and through simulations, we identified several key performance indicators, including the relationship between step length and foot stability, and the effect of different leg designs on this relationship. By testing various configurations, we found that a compact, curved design with propellant storage near the foot performed best. To further optimize the robot's movement, we proposed a controlled retropulse action that could enhance stability during gait by reducing oscillations and making the robot's movement more efficient by 20%.

We establish that for a domain with a proper map to another domain if its underlying topological properties are similar to those of a domain, then its analytical properties will also be comparable to those of a domain.

In order to reduce energy consumption and heat generation, a method called HyperDegrade is proposed, which involves scaling back CPU frequencies across multiple layers of a computer system. This approach aims to take advantage of the relatively low frequency requirements of certain software components. Initially, the proposal involves setting the highest system frequency, which is that of the CPU, to one-third of its original value. This, in turn, leads to reduced frequencies in lower software layers. It is observed that certain software components, including microkernel and hypervisor, can operate at these lower frequencies without significant performance degradation. In the course of this research, an investigation was undertaken to determine the optimal lower frequency for each of these components by dividing existing frequency ranges by three. This resulted in frequencies for various components, which ranged from 13.5 megahertz to 542 megahertz. A simulation of this approach on an Linux-based system revealed a significant reduction in energy consumption of 72%. Additionally, the research includes an offer to share the system's source code with any institution or individual interested in reducing energy consumption through frequency degradation.

We have developed a novel method for simplifying knots, which involves dividing an input knot into three parts: a central subdiagram, surrounded by two surrounding subdiagrams. Our procedure, inspired by a similar technique by a different author, ensures that the original knot can be reassembled from these subdiagrams in a simplified form. Unlike other unknotting methods, this approach does not equate knots with their mirror images and can distinguish between different unknotting formats. Specifically, it applies to both classical and welded knots and provides a new source of invariants for these objects.

We've demonstrated that the Fox-Hatcher loop is a Vassiliev invariant from order two, and it's not equivalent to any 2nd order Vassiliev invariants. Additionally, its distinctiveness is proven with the aid of a specific isogeny induced by a particular group of order three.

In this research, a swarm of simple agents, which are located on an undirected graph and can communicate with neighboring agents, are enabled to collaborate strategically to achieve various objectives. The agents have limited computational powers and can only switch between three states: blocking connections, establishing connections, or remaining neutral. By examining a discrete dynamic model with state transitions, we determined its equivalent continuous counterpart and established the existence of unique solutions for various scenarios. We further proved that in many cases, there are unique equilibria that are stable when the time between state transitions is small. Ultimately, we explored several example applications, demonstrating how the simple, robust collaboration protocol interacts with various environments, and offering potential avenues for further research.

In Federated Learning, a model is trained across multiple entities by a central organizer, taking advantage of data that would otherwise remain inaccessible due to geographical restrictions. Despite potential difficulties, researchers have explored both horizontal and vertical FL scenarios. Although primarily focused on horizontal FL, our research highlights the risks of privacy-based attacks aimed at misleading a model trained in a vertical FL setting, providing evidence of how a malicious participant can manipulate a model trained with encrypted data in a FL scenario characterized by data splitting across different attributes. We also offer suggestions on how to prevent such assaults.

Kernel methods are commonly used in machine learning applications due to their capability to capture non-linear relationships. However, selecting an optimal kernel function can be challenging, as it depends on knowing the underlying data distribution, which is often unknown. As a result, kernel functions are often chosen heuristically, based on past experience, rather than being data-driven. In this research, we propose a novel approach to estimating the optimal kernel function using random Fourier features, which are used to speed up kernel-based methods. When used with a scaling technique, these features enable the automatic selection of kernel functions based on the characteristics of the input data, without requiring additional training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which we call Data Dependent Kernel Estimation (DDKE), in comparing it to traditional methods, including the choice of kernel functions and scaling factors via grid search and Bayesian optimization. DDKE outperforms these comparisons in various machine learning tasks, including classification and regression.

The wreath product of a group H represented by G is defined as the group whose elements are formal linear combinations of permuted copies of H, under the operation determined by multi-linear composition. This paper demonstrates that any group representation into the wreath product of H over G is equivalent to a family of representations of H, attached to distinct sets of symbols, which are themselves represented by G. The paper also shows that two such families of representations are equivalent if and only if the corresponding sets of mapping symbols are in the same orbit under the action of G on the set of all mapping symbols. A specific example is given where H is the symmetric group S3 and G is the cyclic group C4. The paper further introduces the concept of a Cartesian partition as a family of sets indexed by the sets of symbols used in representations of a group, which are themselves represented by that group. The result regarding the equivalence of mapping symbol sets under the action of G on the set of all mapping symbols, can be rephrased as the statement that two Cartesian partitions are in the same orbit if and only if they contain the same number of sets, are isomorphic as sets, and the index of each set in that set is the same when acted upon by G. The paper finally notes that the set of all Cartesian partitions is itself closed under the action of G on the set of all mapping symbols, which induces a group structure on that set of Cartesian partitions, specifically the wreath product of S3 over

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by establishing that if a conformally flat hypersurface has a constant M\"obius curvature under specific symmetry conditions, it can be formed by rotating a conformally flat hypersurface of n-dimensional space around an axis. Conversely, any rotated conformally flat hypersurface of this type is also a conformally flat hypersurface of n+2-dimensional space. We then prove that these conformally flat hypersurfaces all have the same volume and a specific ratio to the volume of a (n+1)-dimensional sphere. We go on to demonstrate that when n is 4 or higher, there are no compact conformally flat hypersurfaces of n+2-dimensional space with a constant M\"obius curvature and a given volume ratio to the volume of a (n+1)-dimensional sphere, except in special cases where the M\"obius curvature can be 0, in which event it is not clear if there are any exceptions, or the volume ratio is less than 1, in which case there are no exceptions.

A new method of efficient wireless communication systems is proposed in a new research format, where data and energy are transmitted through separate frequency bands and power is harvested from the signal received. To analyze this system, a mathematical model with various services and users was developed and efficient management of power and data transmission rates was optimized to maximize the overall performance. Compared to similar, more complex models, this system showed significant improvements in power harvesting and communication efficiency. The proposed model can be applied to various scenarios and even dynamic systems with changing conditions.

Network instability often manifests as destructive waves propagating rapidly and affecting vast areas, as evident in the sizing of avalanches, tree structures, and other systems exhibiting criticality. A collaborative group of researchers from Italy, USA, and Spain has investigated the massive pattern of network instability using the Cayley tree model and Percolation theory. They obtained a precise, universal formula for the size of avalanches, which they have made publicly available.

The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies requires the improvement of response speed in sensors. A novel device called sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is proposed, which combines a Sagnac interferometer with a liquid surface distorting due to gravitational force. With a proposed 10cm liquid radius and 10Hz natural frequency, this device can detect gravitational waves in the range of 100Hz to 300Hz and has a response time 10 times faster than current G-Wave detector technology. A research team from China has successfully demonstrated the operation of a working model with a 5cm liquid radius and 20Hz natural frequency, which detects gravitational waves in the range of 20Hz to 40Hz based on theoretical simulation.

In large-scale MIMO systems, a potential challenge arises when multiple base stations have close proximity to each other, as their co-located antennas may create overlapping coverage areas, leading to non-trivial visibility regions and potential interference problems. As a result, determining effective and fair management protocols to minimize interference and ensure fair coexistence has become a crucial research need.
